About: Newton's First Law — Inertia

Source

Lecture
Introductory classical mechanics — Newtonian dynamics (Newton's first law of motion: inertia).
Simulation
"Newton's First Law — Inertia": a single 1-D scene — a puck coasting on frictionless ice with Fnet = 0, plus a labeled ⚠ Aristotle counterfactual for contrast.
Concept
Force changes motion — it does not sustain it: Fnet = 0 ⇒ constant velocity, with rest just the v = 0 special case.
Serves
Zero net force ⇒ constant v (not rest), with balanced mg/N arrows drawn and the ⚠ Aristotle counterfactual available for contrast.
Inquiry
Does v change while Fnet = 0? What speed does the puck keep after F returns to 0?
Misconception
"If an object is moving there must be a net force pushing it along" — zero net force means constant velocity, not rest.

Newton's First Law

Guided Inquiry

1 · Meet Law ① — Fnet = 0

The puck coasts right at 2 m/s on ice. Red mg ↓ and blue N ↑ cancel, so horizontal Fnet = 0; the green arrow is velocity. Watch the v readout (press ▶ Play if paused) — does it budge?

2 · Predict — what does v do?

Run time forward with Fnet = 0. What does the puck’s velocity do?

3 · When does velocity change?

Drag F to +4 N for a moment, then back to 0 N. Exactly when does v change — and what speed does the puck keep once F is 0 again? Watch the v readout and the green arrow. Then flip to ⚠ Aristotle: what happens the instant F returns to 0?

4 · Law ① in one line

Velocity changes only while a net force acts — and stays exactly constant the moment Fnet returns to 0. Rest is just the v = 0 case. Explore freely: nudge F, flip ⚠ Aristotle to visit the world your gut expected, and watch the v readout tell the truth.

① Law of inertia

F_net = 0 ⇔ dv/dt = 0

Zero net force means velocity is constant — any constant, not necessarily zero. Rest (v = 0) is just one special case. On the puck, mg and N cancel: balanced forces ⇒ no change of motion.

⚠ The counterfactual (for contrast)

v = F/k (k = 2 N·s/m)

⚠ Aristotle: force sustains velocity — F = 0 ⇒ instant rest. It is implemented exactly so you can watch it fail.

Newton's First Law

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A hockey puck sits on frictionless ice. The sim draws the forces on it and its velocity as arrows, so you can ask what a force does to the way the puck moves.

What you'll learn

  • Which forces act on the puck and how to find the net force from them.
  • How to read the velocity and the net force from the arrows and the readouts.
  • How Newton's idea of force compares with the rival idea the sim calls Aristotle's.
A puck of mass m on ice. The ice pushes up with N, gravity pulls down with mg, F is the applied force, and v is the velocity.

What's on screen

  • The puck on ice: a side view. The ruler scrolls past below it, so the puck stays near the left of the scene.
  • N: the blue arrow up, the normal force from the ice.
  • mg: the red arrow down, the weight. Both arrows keep one fixed length, so read their labels for the numbers.
  • F: the amber arrow along the ice. It appears only when the applied force is not zero.
  • v: the green arrow above the puck, its velocity. It is a dot when the puck is at rest.
See itOpen the sim with the puck on the ice at t = 0, paused. Watch for: the blue N arrow, the red mg arrow, and the green v arrow above the puck.

03

The forces on the puck are its weight, the normal force and F

Three forces can act on the puck. Gravity pulls it down with its weight mg. The ice pushes up on it with a normal force N. The slider sets the applied force F, which acts along the ice.

The sim always makes N equal to mg, so for m = 4 kg both labels read 39.2 N. These two forces cancel, which leaves F as the only force along the ice. The net force is the vector sum of all the forces on the puck:

F⃗net = F⃗ + N⃗ + m g⃗, so along the ice Fnet = F
The sim's Fnet readout is this horizontal sum.
  • The ice has no friction, so nothing else acts along the ice.
  • Zero net force is not the same as no forces. mg and N are both present while they cancel.
See itSet the mass to 4 kg and look at the two labels. Watch for: N and mg both reading 39.2 N.
04

Zero net force means the velocity stays constant

Newton's first law says that a body on which the net force is zero keeps its velocity, in size and in direction. The sim's Formal strip writes it as

F⃗net = 0 ⟺ v⃗ = constant
Both directions hold: constant velocity means zero net force.

With F = 0 the puck keeps v = 2.00 m/s at every instant. It covers 20 m in one 10 s run, and it would keep going if the ice were longer. Nothing has to push it.

  • Constant does not mean zero. Rest, v = 0, is just the special case.
  • Inertia is this tendency to keep the velocity. It is a property of the body, not a force.
  • The law holds in an inertial frame, one that is not accelerating.
See itRun the puck with F = 0 and watch the Data panel. Watch for: v = 2.00 m/s in the readout while t and x keep counting up.
05

A net force changes the velocity, and the new velocity is kept

When Fnet is not zero the velocity changes. In the Newton model the puck accelerates at

a = Fnet / m, v = v0 + a t
Valid while Fnet stays constant.

Push with F = +4 N on the 1 kg puck for 0.5 s. Then a = 4 m/s², and v goes from 2.00 to 4.00 m/s. The moment F returns to 0, a is 0 again and the puck keeps 4.00 m/s. A force opposite to the motion slows it: with F = −4 N, v reaches 0 at t = 0.5 s.

For a 1 kg puck the 4 N push lasts 0.5 s. The velocity changes only while it acts.
See itPush with +4 N for half a second of sim time, then return F to 0. Watch for: v rising from 2 to about 4 m/s and then holding there.
06

A larger mass changes its velocity more slowly

The mass sets how much a given force changes the velocity. Since a = Fnet/m, the same push on a puck four times as heavy gives one quarter of the acceleration.

  • F = +4 N for 0.5 s on 1 kg: v rises by 2.00 m/s, to 4.00 m/s.
  • The same push on 4 kg: a = 1 m/s², and v rises by 0.50 m/s, to 2.50 m/s.

Mass measures the puck's inertia: how strongly it resists a change of velocity. With F = 0 the mass does not matter. The puck coasts at 2.00 m/s whatever m is.

F m

These sliders move the sim too.

See itGive the same +4 N push to the 4 kg puck. Watch for: v rising only a little, to about 2.5 m/s.
07

The Aristotle model makes force hold the velocity

The ⚠ Aristotle button runs a rival rule that the sim marks as wrong, so that you can watch it fail. In it the velocity follows the force:

v = F / k, k = 2 N·s/m
Force sustains the speed. There is no acceleration.

At F = 0 this model gives v = 0, so the puck stops the instant it is switched on. At F = +4 N it gives a steady 2.00 m/s, and at +10 N a steady 5.00 m/s. In the Newton model the same 4 N push piles up speed, reaching 10.0 m/s after 2 s on the 1 kg puck.

The rule feels right because on a floor a sliding box does stop unless you keep pushing. The cause is friction, a hidden force opposing the motion. The ice removes it, and the Newton model fits.

See itSwitch to the Aristotle model with F = 0. Watch for: v dropping to 0.00 m/s and the chip ⚠ Aristotle v = F/k at the top left.
08

Where it matters

  • Seat belts. When a car stops suddenly, a passenger with nothing to hold them keeps the car's old velocity. The belt supplies the force that changes it.
  • The tablecloth trick. A cloth is pulled out so quickly that friction acts on the dishes for only a moment. They hardly gain any velocity and stay almost where they were.
  • Coasting spacecraft. Far from any planet, with the engine off, a probe feels almost no net force. Its velocity stays nearly constant for years.
  • Inertial frames. In a bus that is braking, a loose ball rolls forward with no push on it. The first law does not hold in that frame, so the bus is not an inertial frame.
09

Summary

In one line. Newton's first law says what the net force on a body decides about its velocity.

Key points

  • F⃗net = 0 ⟺ v⃗ is constant. Rest is the case v = 0.
  • While Fnet acts, a = Fnet/m. When it returns to 0, the velocity it reached is kept.
  • Mass measures inertia. In the Aristotle model v = F/k fails, because it ignores the hidden friction force.

Common mix-ups

  • "A moving body must have a net force on it." Only a change of velocity needs a net force. At constant velocity it is zero.
  • "Zero net force means no forces." mg and N are both there. Their sum is zero.
  • "Inertia is a force that keeps the puck going." It is a property of the body. It resists changes, and it does not push.

Things to try on your own

  • Give F = +4 N for 0.5 s to the 8 kg puck and predict v from a = F/m before you read it.
  • Set F = −4 N on the 1 kg puck and note the time at which v passes through 0.
  • Set F = +10 N and m = 0.5 kg, and compare v after 1 s in the Newton and Aristotle models.
